exemplar: The passage argues that industrialization fundamentally changed American labor: skilled craft work gave way to machine-tended factory jobs, concentrating workers in cities and sharpening conflict between capital and labor.

Andrew Carnegie's steel empire used the Bessemer process to mass-produce cheap steel, building a vertically integrated corporation that dominated the industry and made Carnegie the richest man in America.

Workers fought back through unions: the Knights of Labor organized skilled and unskilled workers alike in the 1880s, and the American Federation of Labor built powerful craft unions that struck for higher wages and shorter hours.
parts: A. Briefly describe ONE claim the passage makes about how industrialization changed American work.
B. Briefly explain how ONE specific technological or business innovation contributed to industrial growth.
C. Briefly explain ONE way workers responded to industrial working conditions.

stimulus.attribution: Original historian-style passage written for this item.
stimulus.text: Between 1865 and 1900, historians argue, industrialization remade the American economy and American life. New technologies - the Bessemer process for steel, the telephone, electric light - combined with new business forms like the corporation and the trust to create an economy of unprecedented scale. Millions of Americans left farms and crossed oceans to tend machines in factories, mines, and mills. Industrialization made the United States the world's leading manufacturing nation, but it also concentrated immense wealth in a few hands, subjected workers to dangerous and monotonous labor, and sparked decades of bitter conflict between capital and labor.

exemplar: Henry argues that the colonies have exhausted every peaceful means of redress - petitions, remonstrances, supplications - and that Britain has answered only with violence, so war is now unavoidable.
The Intolerable Acts (1774), which closed Boston's port and revoked Massachusetts' charter after the Tea Party, convinced many colonists that Parliament intended to destroy their liberties.

Henry's speech helped push Virginia toward independence: the convention authorized its delegates to propose independence, leading to Richard Henry Lee's resolution in the Continental Congress in June 1776.
parts: A. Briefly describe Henry's argument for war in the excerpt.
B. Briefly explain ONE British action between 1763 and 1775 that pushed colonists toward Henry's position.
C. Briefly explain ONE effect of speeches like Henry's on the movement for independence.

stimulus.attribution: Patrick Henry, speech to the Virginia Convention, Richmond, March 23, 1775.
stimulus.text: I know not what course others may take; but as for me, give me liberty or give me death!

exemplar: The painting romanticizes the Pilgrims' departure as a solemn, heroic embarkation - a founding moment of religious liberty and national origins, painted for the nation's Capitol.
The Pilgrims sought religious freedom as Separatists, but they also sought economic opportunity: their voyage was funded by merchant investors expecting profit from American resources.

The painting's heroic framing omits the Native perspective entirely: within a generation, English expansion would bring devastating war - King Philip's War (1675-1676) - to the peoples who had helped the colonists survive.
parts: A. Briefly describe how the painting portrays the Pilgrims' departure.
B. Briefly explain ONE motive, besides religion, that drew English colonists to New England.
C. Briefly explain ONE way the painting's heroic portrayal of colonization is incomplete.

stimulus.attribution: Described from Robert Walter Weir's Embarkation of the Pilgrims (1843), in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol.
stimulus.text: The large painting shows the Pilgrims gathered on a beach at Delftshaven in 1620, preparing to board the Speedwell. Families kneel in prayer around their minister while onlookers watch; ships wait offshore. The scene is solemn and reverent, presenting the departure as a sacred national founding.
